theme: The Incentive Travel Debate: does destination choice actually move the needle on performance?

linkedin.text:
A take from 1,500+ events that might be unpopular:

The destination is almost never the reason an incentive trip succeeds or fails.

We've produced programs in 130+ destinations across 16 years — alpine lodges, coastal villas, city buyouts, private islands. The variable that predicts business impact every single time isn't geography.

It's program architecture.

The three factors that actually move performance metrics:

1. Qualifying criteria that's ambitious, specific and communicated early — so earning the trip means something
2. A program rhythm that balances genuine leisure with moments of intentional business connection
3. Senior leadership presence that signals the trip matters at the highest level

Swap out any one of those three for a more impressive destination and the ROI collapses.

For Sales, HR and Marketing leaders who've run incentive programs: do you agree? Or has destination been the determining factor in your experience?

I'm genuinely interested in where people land on this — drop your take below.

instagram.text:
Hot take: the destination is rarely the reason an incentive trip succeeds. 🌍

We've produced incentive programs across 130+ destinations over 16 years.

The trips that move the needle on sales performance and retention come down to:

↳ How well qualifying criteria was set and communicated
↳ Whether the program had business rhythm, not just leisure
↳ Whether leadership actually showed up

The destination opens the door. Program design decides what walks through it.

HR and Sales leaders — has a destination ever made or broken an incentive trip for your team? Comment below or DM us. We'd love to hear it.

facebook.text:
Hot take from 16 years of incentive travel production:

The destination is rarely the reason a trip succeeds.

We've run incentive programs from the Maldives to Patagonia to the Amalfi Coast. The trips that generate the most business impact — stronger sales pipelines, higher retention signals, genuine team realignment — usually come down to three things that have nothing to do with the destination:

1. How well the qualifying criteria was communicated in advance
2. Whether the program had a clear business rhythm (not just leisure)
3. How leaders showed up during the experience

The destination opens the door. The design of the program decides what walks through it.

What's your take? Have you seen a destination make or break an incentive trip? Tell us below — we're genuinely curious.
